lesson.subtitle: Lesson 11 -- Telling the Story: What Was Happening When It Happened
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Dejair Caitano do Nascimento | Lesson 11 -- Telling the Story
lesson.grammar_point: past continuous for background action interrupted by past simple

listenings.text: Something happened at my first international congress, and I still tell the story. I was standing at my poster on the second morning, and almost nobody was stopping. Everybody was walking past me towards the big posters at the end of the row. So I was reading my own abstract again, only to look busy. Then I noticed one woman. She was not looking at the whole poster. She was looking at one small figure in the corner, for two or three minutes, and while she was looking, she was writing something in her notebook. The thing is, that was the figure I almost removed the week before. She was from a group in Lisbon, they had the same problem with dosage, and we published together two years later. So my advice is simple. When nobody is stopping, do not pause your work and do not look at the floor. Watch who is looking, and talk to that person.

I want to tell you about the worst five minutes of my professional life, because they became the best. I was presenting in a small room, maybe thirty people, and I was speaking much too fast. While I was explaining my second slide, an older man in the front row was shaking his head. Every time I said a number, he was shaking his head again. I realized I was talking only to him, and I was losing the rest of the room. So I stopped. I paused, I drank some water, and I asked him directly. You disagree. Tell me why. And the reaction of the whole room changed. He was not disagreeing with my data. He was disagreeing with my units. I had milligrams where I needed micrograms. Meanwhile, everybody else was too polite to say it. That man saved my paper. So when you notice a reaction like that, do not continue. Ask.
